https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Using AI in the global fight against HIV
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: When faced with the possibility of an HIV diagnosis, sometimes the best initial prescription is support from a trusted friend—someone who might offer not just emotional guidance but also critical, practical health resources. A Harvard research team thinks artificial intelligence has a role to play in that process.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing foods
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) show stronger responses in the brain's reward network when viewing images of appetizing foods—and these brain responses are linked to increases in body fat one year later.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI breast cancer survival model could improve accuracy and personalize care
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: New University of Cincinnati Cancer Center research published in the Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice describes the potential for a more robust and accurate breast cancer survival model that combines statistical methods with a deep learning framework. The goal is to give physicians a better tool to make personalized care decisions for each patient.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: How a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body's chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: The tendency to imitate others is shared across 22 countries, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: People often imitate some of the actions and gestures of others they are observing, without deliberately trying to do so. This tendency, known as automatic imitation, has long been assumed to be universal.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Who decides when medical AI may be updated?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Medical AI can improve with new patient data, but every update must be checked first. Patients, equipment and ways of working change, and a model trained on older data can gradually get worse without anyone noticing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: How much autonomy do women actually have when giving birth?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: You spend your pregnancy researching and planning for when your baby finally arrives, as well as considering what might happen if things don't go according to plan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: 4 ways to help your body adjust to the fall time change
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the fall time change automatically, our body clock isn't quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Women are more optimistic about aging—until memory problems emerge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: A study, published in the Journal of Women & Aging, found memory complaints were linked to negative expectations about aging in people with mild cognitive impairment as well as cognitively healthy adults.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Updated cancer treatment framework offers new guidance on actionability and resistance biomarkers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: ESMO has published version 2 of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), a major update to the internationally recognized precision oncology framework that helps oncologists assess the clinical relevance of molecular alterations and match patients with the most appropriate targeted therapies.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Can Reddit help strengthen health communications on extreme heat?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Two years ago, Robbie M. Parks, an environmental health scientist at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and Nathaniel Matthews-Trigg, director of climate and disaster resilience at Americares, founded an online community on Reddit, r/heat_prep, where members share information and advice about coping with extreme temperatures.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Blood test can help clinicians better identify brain injury severity in patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: Clinician-scientists hope to expand the use of blood-based biomarker tests for traumatic brain injury (TBI) to improve identification and escalation of care for patients whose diagnosis otherwise might be missed.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.title: First-of-its-kind trial tests low-dose radiation to target brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease. The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.

https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.summary: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.summary: Political campaigns often use fear to play on voters’ existing prejudices and stereotypes. What that means for your vote is less predictable.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.title: Habitat explains Finnish animal distributions better than climate, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.summary: Researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to understand which is the dominant factor for species occurrence and abundance: the climate or habitat-related variables, such as their natural state and the share of land shaped by human activity. Solutions to mitigate biodiversity loss depend on the answer to this question.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.summary: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.title: Study maps the human side of flood risk
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.summary: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.summary: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.title: 'It's pretty toxic… but just a little, I want to be like that': What young men think of manosphere content
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.summary: Masculinity content promises young men self-optimization and success, but often delivers health harms, risk-taking, unattainable standards, gender stereotypes and misogyny. The latter is the strongest predictor of violent extremism.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists demonstrate AI-designed enzyme for drug synthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: The new RFD4-Proteina unified generative model for protein design—created by the Institute for Protein Design (IPD) in collaboration with NVIDIA—uses advanced AI to generate entirely new protein sequences and structures, achieving computational design success rates five to 10 times higher than previous models and generating candidates five to 10 times faster.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.title: Chemically modified sugars enable direct nanostructure formation
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.summary: Researchers at AIST have demonstrated the synthesis of nanoporous carbonaceous materials and carbonaceous materials with layered nanostructures through a simple process involving the chemical modification of common sugars such as sucrose and fructose.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.title: The psychology of why we overpay for used cars—study points to left-digit bias
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.summary: Consumers routinely ignore information when making purchases. They overlook the tax attached to a price, skim past ingredient lists and often fail to process exact numbers with any precision.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.title: Designing better adsorbents to remove PFAS from water
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.summary: A review by Tohoku University researchers identifies key molecular features that could guide the development of more effective materials for removing PFAS from water. The study is published in the journal ACS Materials Au.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.summary: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..title: Elections are more predictable than they look
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..summary: As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.title: Bacteria reinvent their weapons through selection, chance and gene swapping
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.summary: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). They are produced by large bacterial enzyme machineries—the nonribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These function like molecular assembly lines: Similar to the stations in a car factory, where new parts are added to the car at each step, several specialized modules string together amino acid by amino acid to build a peptide.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.title: New marker panel and free web tool help track stem cells as they develop
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.summary: How can the identity of pluripotent stem cells be determined more reliably during their differentiation? Researchers from the IUF—Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine and Heinrich Heine University Duesseldorf have systematically validated marker genes for this purpose and developed a web-based application for the automated classification of early cell fates. The study has been published in Stem Cell Reports.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.title: Can we stop antibiotic resistance from ruining promising drugs before they reach patients?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.summary: What if we could predict early in drug development which antibiotics bacteria are most likely to become resistant to? In a review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, researchers from the HUN-REN Biological Research Centre, Szeged (HUN-REN BRC Szeged) and the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine (HCEMM) in Szeged propose a five-step decision-making framework that could help identify resistance risks early, refine promising drug candidates and prevent costly failures.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.summary: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.title: Everyday Mylar turned into a promising insulator for lunar habitats
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.summary: Establishing a long-term presence on the moon will require solving challenges that are easy to overlook on Earth. Lunar temperatures, for instance, can vary from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling, making effective insulation essential for lunar habitats.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.title: Chaos makes sense of market movements in a crisis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.summary: Research shows that crises do more than cause financial market volatility and falling share prices—they lead to markets becoming far more interconnected.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.title: Stellar collision may explain why Orion Nebula's planet-forming disks appear younger than its stars
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.summary: The Orion Nebula is a large star-forming region visible to the naked eye. Some of the young stars in the nebula are surrounded by disks of gas and dust in which planets form. Radiation from the massive central star, 1 Ori C1 (Theta-1 Orionis C1), gradually strips material from these disks, giving them shapes that resemble tadpoles.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.title: Mechanism behind PARP1-mediated DNA repair characterized, offering insight into targeted cancer therapy
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.summary: When DNA is damaged, cellular processes respond and repair the DNA. Inhibiting DNA damage repair can be therapeutically beneficial in cancers with genetic vulnerabilities related to DNA damage response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have uncovered a mechanism behind how this process works, which may have implications for cancer treatment. The results were published today in Molecular Cell.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.title: Rare fossils reveal what ancient Denisovans may have looked like
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.summary: Whenever anything is written about the Denisovans, the word "mysterious" is almost guaranteed to appear. That is because we just don't know a lot about this extinct human group that may have lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago and was closely related to the Neanderthals. The main reason for that is a sparse fossil record.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.summary: Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could the opposite happen: could a single black hole split into two smaller ones? That question is explored in a new theoretical study: "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," published in the journal Physical Review D.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.title: Hoarders without borders: Study suggests investors aid international expansion
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.summary: Venture capital firms can help young businesses expand internationally by providing funding as well as market knowledge, expertise and access to professional networks, according to a research literature review published in the International Journal of Management and Enterprise Development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.summary: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.title: As flood risk rises, some communities question the idea of resilience
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.summary: Climate change is increasing flood risk across the U.K. As floods become more frequent and intense, communities are increasingly encouraged to become resilient and "live with water." Yet in some flood-prone areas, residents are rejecting these calls, concerned that resilience is less about helping communities and more about transferring responsibility from institutions to citizens.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.title: Paleolithic human DNA reveals east-west connections across Ice Age Europe
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.summary: More than 30,000 years ago, people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian) were more interconnected than previously thought. An international research team led by the University of Vienna has uncovered new genetic evidence of long-distance connections between these populations. Published in Science Advances, the study combines genomic data from rare human remains with human DNA preserved in cave sediments.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists find key to predicting some El Niño events 12 months ahead
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Scientists have identified the conditions that make it possible to predict some El Niño and La Niña events up to a year in advance, potentially giving communities and decision-makers significantly more time to prepare for weather extremes.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.title: AI is solving math problems that stumped humans. What comes next?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.summary: A few short years ago, asking AI to add two four-digit numbers together for a third-grade math assignment would have been a bad idea. Over half the time, the answer would be wrong, studies have shown. Long division or a "leaky tank" problem, an algebra class staple? Forget about it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Diagnostic test could help doctors refine prostate cancer treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men—in 2013, it affected more than 1 million men across the world. The cancer does not behave the same way in every patient, and doctors have long faced a difficult balancing act between identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive treatment and those who may do just as well without it. Treating someone more aggressively than necessary is associated with increased side effects and poorer quality of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Reprogramming tumor microenvironment could improve prospects for treatment of pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat cancers. One reason for its resistance to therapy is the dense tissue surrounding the tumor that acts as a protective barrier and suppresses the immune response. It is a complex tissue made of supporting cells, blood vessels and immune cells—the tumor microenvironment. In pancreatic cancer, this surrounding tissue accounts for up to 90% of the tumor mass.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tegoprubart preserves kidney function better than tacrolimus in first-time transplant patients, trial suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: The phase 2 BESTOW clinical trial showed that tegoprubart (a novel anti-CD40L antibody therapy) was better at preserving kidney function than tacrolimus (the current standard of care) in immunosuppressive regimens in adults receiving their first kidney transplant. Kidney graft function stabilized after the first month of treatment and remained higher in tegoprubart-treated patients than in tacrolimus-treated patients at each reported time point, with a statistically significant kidney function benefit at 18 months. A recent analysis of BESTOW data found that tegoprubart also caused greater improvements in patient-reported health-related quality of life compared with tacrolimus in study parti

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.title: US–Mexico border counties face high kidney disease–related mortality and low nephrologist availability
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.summary: New research indicates that U.S.–Mexico border counties experience disproportionately elevated rates of death from chronic kidney disease (CKD), alongside reduced availability of nephrologists. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Standard kidney function tests underestimate chronic kidney disease in people with cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: New research indicates that commonly used measures of kidney function underestimate the prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in patients with cancer. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Melanoma vaccine reduces death or cancer recurrence by 42%
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: In a world-first international trial, adding intismeran, a type of personalized therapeutic cancer vaccine made from each patient's own tumor, to pembrolizumab immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: 5 great cardio workouts you can do at home
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: You might have heard that cardio, or aerobic, exercise is one of the best ways to keep your heart, lungs and cardiovascular system healthy and strong.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Online resources and coaching helped people seek genetic testing for cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.summary: About 10% of cancers are linked to an inherited genetic variant, but as few as one in 15 cancer patients eligible for genetic testing complete it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Study identifies potential new treatment targets for the most common type of bowel cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Research published today identifies potential new ways to treat the most common type of colorectal cancer in Ireland. The study, conducted by an international research team led by RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences and The Institute of Cancer Research, London, provides a roadmap for repurposing existing drugs and developing new ones to create more effective, personalized treatments for thousands of patients who currently have limited options.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.title: A third of young adults turn to AI for substance-use information
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.summary: More than 32% of participants in a Rutgers study reported using ChatGPT and similar chatbots for substance-use information.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Could fish consumption reduce the risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: A new prospective study from Japan explored whether fish consumption before and during pregnancy is linked to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. Researchers analyzed data from women in Japan, examining fish consumption and n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) intake across different stages of pregnancy. The results reveal a pattern that may have implications for preconception and prenatal nutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mental health disparities persist for LGBTQ+ college students nationwide, largest study of its kind finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: LGBTQ+ college students who experience discrimination are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts and to avoid needed health care, according to a new national study by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, Boston University School of Public Health and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute. The findings underscore the impact of discrimination on student mental health during a critical stage of life. The results are published in the journal Behavioral Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: ESMO: New analysis reinforces survival benefits of targeted therapy for advanced pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: A new analysis of a phase 3 clinical trial found that the targeted drug daraxonrasib improved survival compared with standard chemotherapy across multiple groups of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, including those with different RAS mutations and those without an identified RAS mutation.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Six-gene scoring system could help predict leukemia survival
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: The activity of six different genes can help determine survival in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), according to a study published in Science Advances. The findings by researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) in Barcelona lay the foundations for new ways of predicting how patients will fare with a type of blood cancer that has widely variable outcomes from one patient to the next.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How cancers evade chemotherapy by entering a 'zombie-like state'
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Scientists at Trinity College Dublin have made a breakthrough in understanding how cancer cells can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter a "zombie-like state," called premature senescence, that can attract the wound-healing properties of the immune system.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cancer cells' own carbon monoxide fuels anticancer drug production in lab tests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: What if we could use a cancer's own byproduct to make drugs that destroy tumor cells from the inside? That is what Katsunori Tanaka and his team have done at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Procedure standard/procedure guideline for ventilation–perfusion pulmonary scintigraphy published
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI), European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM), American College of Nuclear Medicine (ACNM) and Australian and New Zealand Society of Nuclear Medicine (ANZSNM) have issued a new procedure standard/procedure guideline for performing and interpreting lung imaging studies. The standard/guideline, published in the September issue of The Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology, provides a framework for clinical applications and standardization of ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, ventilation-only scintigraphy and perfusion-only scintigraphy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Real-world results confirm benefit of antigen therapy for prostate cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is safe and effective for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) in routine clinical practice, consistent with outcomes from the VISION trial. An analysis of outcomes from a French early-access program, the largest real-world cohort of patients studied to date, confirms the benefit-risk profile of the therapy, while also shedding light on patient selection and use trends. This research was published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: FDA approves hepatitis B shot that may let some patients stop all treatment

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Researchers at the University of Vermont have discovered a surprising pattern in human language that challenges a scientific theory widely accepted for more than 70 years. Their findings suggest that the meaning of words is shaped by something more fundamental than emotion: our understanding of power, danger, and order. The study, published in Science Advances , introduces a new approach called "ousiometrics," which uses mathematical methods to measure the essential meaning of language. Its most striking finding is that the words people use show a consistent and widespread preference for safety over danger. This hidden safety bias could transform how researchers study language, understand human behavior, and develop artificial intelligence systems that interpret what people say and write. Since the 1950s, much of the scientific understanding of word meaning has relied on a framework developed through pioneering research by psychologist Charles Osgood and others. Known as the VAD model, it describes meaning through three emotional dimensions: valence (positive vs. negative), arousal (excited vs. calm), and dominance (controlling vs. submissive). This approach became influential in psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in systems designed to identify the emotional tone of written language. However, the University of Vermont researchers found evidence that this long-established model overlooks important aspects of how meaning is organized. Their analysis examined billions of individual uses of more than 20,000 words across a wide range of real-world texts. Using advanced computational techniques, the team identified a different underlying structure. They found that the three dimensions in the traditional VAD model are not independent of one another, as previously assumed. Instead, their results indicate that word meaning can be more effectively described through three separate dimensions: power (weak vs. powerful), danger (safe vs. dangerous), and structure (ordered vs. chaotic). The research, supported by the US National Science Foundation, Google, MassMutual, and other funders, found that this new framework accounted for more than 90% of the variation in measured word meaning. The traditional VAD approach explained approximately 72%. That improvement could be especially important as large language models, automated content moderation, and other AI technologies increasingly depend on understanding human communication. One of the study's most unexpected discoveries emerged when the researchers examined how words actually appear in everyday communication. Across books, news reporting, social media, and spoken language, words associated with safety appeared much more frequently than those associated with danger. This finding offers a new explanation for a familiar phenomenon called the Pollyanna principle, which describes the tendency for human language to lean toward positive rather than negative words. For decades, researchers generally interpreted this pattern as evidence that people favor positive emotional expressions. The new analysis suggests that something more fundamental may be responsible. According to the researchers, the apparent preference for positivity largely reflects an underlying preference for safety. "The Pollyanna principle's positivity bias," the study concludes. "is, in fact, a one-dimensional projection of an underlying safety bias." "This is a big observation that comes out of this work," said Peter Dodds, director of the UVM's Complex Systems Institute and senior author of the study. "Expressions of safety are crucial to all language." The discovery raises an intriguing possibility: the structure of human language may reflect evolutionary pressures associated with staying alive. From this perspective, words do more than communicate feelings. They also help people recognize threats, evaluate uncertainty, establish trust, and coordinate actions with others. Being able to distinguish between safety and danger is essential to survival. The researchers suggest that this basic human priority may also influence how meaning is organized in language. Throughout daily life, people constantly exchange information about whether individuals, places, situations, and behaviors are threatening or safe. The new findings suggest that these distinctions may be more central to communication than previously recognized. They also offer a different interpretation of why positive language is so common. Rather than simply expressing happiness or approval, many positive words may convey a sense of security, stability, or predictability. Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher in UVM's Computational Story Lab and a co-author of the study, said the three newly identified dimensions reflect experiences that are fundamental to human life. "Power, danger, and structure," she said, "are relevant to every person that's ever lived." Researchers have also long recognized that people tend to favor language associated with goodness and low aggression. The team argues that these familiar tendencies may arise from the same deeper pattern. "We now understand," the team writes, that these are "shadows of an underlying linguistic safety bias." Although the results are consistent with a possible connection between language and survival, they do not establish that evolutionary pressures directly caused the safety bias. The findings have implications that extend well beyond linguistics. Many artificial intelligence systems use sentiment analysis to determine whether language expresses positive, negative, or neutral feelings. Some approaches also draw on the traditional VAD framework to measure emotional meaning. If that framework does not fully capture the underlying structure of language, systems built around it could overlook important distinctions in what people communicate. The researchers suggest that incorporating power, danger, and structure could eventually help AI models interpret language more accurately and explain their assessments more clearly. This may be particularly useful when analyzing trust, risk, and decision-making. In linguistics, the findings offer a different way to understand the foundations of meaning. Instead of treating emotional tone as the primary organizing principle, the new framework emphasizes distinctions related to strength, safety, and predictability. Psychology could also be affected. Decades of studies have used the VAD model to investigate emotions, perception, and behavior. A different set of fundamental dimensions could encourage researchers to reconsider how some of those findings are interpreted. The discovery may also interest neuroscientists. The human brain is highly sensitive to threats and signals of safety, and the newly identified linguistic bias suggests that these biological priorities may be reflected in language. This potential connection could help researchers explore relationships between brain activity and symbolic communication, although further research would be needed to establish them. To investigate these patterns, the researchers created analytical methods designed to measure meaning across enormous collections of written and spoken language. One of their central innovations is the "ousiometer," a tool that rapidly evaluates the essential meaning of large bodies of text and produces an average meaning score. (The word "ouisa" comes from Ancient Greek and is a root for the English word "essence.") The ousiometer builds on an earlier tool developed by the research team called the "hedonometer" (a happiness meter). While that instrument measures the overall emotional tone of language, the new approach examines broader patterns of meaning. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home. Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication. The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension , a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best. The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure. By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure. The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic. The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels. Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself. Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week. The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home. However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device. Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension. A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment. This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness. Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said: "This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham. "As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension." High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time. Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment. This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies. Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients. For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. Scientists believe it represents the earliest known example of flight loss in birds, overturning assumptions about how these animals evolved.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A remarkably preserved 150-million-year-old bird fossil discovered in China is challenging long-standing ideas about how birds evolved. Rather than developing increasingly sophisticated flight abilities, some of the earliest birds appear to have taken a very different evolutionary path, including losing the ability to fly altogether. The newly identified species, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis , lived during the Late Jurassic period (150-148 million years ago). Described in a study published in Nature, the crow-sized creature provides evidence that early bird evolution was much more complex than scientists once believed. Instead of evolving primarily to become better flyers, ancient birds were adapting to a variety of environments and ways of life, including those that favored living on the ground. Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and the Fujian Institute of Geological Sciences uncovered the fossil in the recently recognized Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province in southeastern China. According to their findings, Yuezhuornis represents the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its ability to fly. One of the most remarkable features of Yuezhuornis is its unusual combination of bird and dinosaur characteristics. Although it possessed skeletal features associated with birds, it also retained anatomical traits that would have been familiar among small predatory dinosaurs. Its jaws contained closely spaced, serrated teeth resembling those of deinonychosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs that included agile predators related to birds. Such teeth are not normally associated with early birds. Even more striking was its second toe, which could bend backward unusually far and carried a curved, sickle-shaped claw. This specialized feature is strongly associated with deinonychosaurs, including dromaeosaurids and troodontids, two groups of predatory dinosaurs. "When we examined Yuezhuornis , we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features," said Dr. Min Wang, corresponding author of the study. "It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized." To understand how Yuezhuornis was related to other prehistoric birds and dinosaurs, scientists carried out detailed analyses of its evolutionary relationships. They used two approaches, maximum parsimony and Bayesian tip-dating, to compare anatomical characteristics and reconstruct the species' position on the evolutionary tree. Maximum parsimony identifies evolutionary relationships that require the fewest changes in characteristics, while Bayesian tip-dating also incorporates statistical estimates of evolutionary history and information about when fossils lived. Both methods produced consistent results, placing Yuezhuornis within Avialae, the evolutionary group that includes modern birds and their closest extinct relatives. "The results consistently placed Yuezhuornis firmly within Avialae (the group containing modern birds and their closest extinct relatives), just crownward of Archaeopteryx and as a sister taxon to Zhengheornis," said Dr. Zhonghe Zhou, a co-author of the study. This placement is particularly important because Archaeopteryx, which also lived roughly 150 million years ago, is among the most famous early bird relatives. The findings indicate that Yuezhuornis belonged to an early branch of bird evolution rather than simply being a small predatory dinosaur with bird-like characteristics. The researchers also examined how Yuezhuornis might have lived. Using measurements of its skeletal proportions and statistical comparisons with other animals, they investigated whether its anatomy was better suited for flying or moving along the ground. The results showed that its limb proportions closely resembled those of modern ground-dwelling birds and certain other prehistoric dinosaurs closely related to birds. This similarity suggests that Yuezhuornis spent its life on the ground and was likely unable to fly. The findings point to an unexpected development in the history of birds. Rather than simply progressing toward stronger wings and more efficient flight, some early bird lineages appear to have moved in the opposite direction, adapting to lifestyles in which flying was no longer necessary. This challenges the traditional assumption that the earliest stages of bird evolution were driven primarily by the demands of flight. Instead, birds were already exploring different ecological roles and developing a surprisingly wide range of body forms. The discovery of Yuezhuornis suggests that the evolution of birds was never a simple, one-directional process. Even during the Late Jurassic, when the earliest bird lineages were emerging, some species were developing adaptations that favored life on land rather than in the air. Its unusual combination of bird-like anatomy, dinosaur-style predatory features, and apparent flightlessness provides a revealing glimpse into that evolutionary experimentation. The fossil shows that early birds were more anatomically and ecologically diverse than previously recognized. It also underscores the scientific importance of the Zhenghe Fauna, a fossil assemblage that is helping researchers investigate a poorly understood period in bird evolution. As additional discoveries emerge from this region of China, scientists may gain an even clearer picture of the surprising evolutionary paths taken by the earliest birds. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A new analysis from Monash University suggests that low-dose aspirin may be linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia in older adults with certain genetic characteristics. Researchers found that people with a specific genetic profile who took aspirin had a 70 percent lower relative risk of developing dementia, raising the possibility that genetic testing could eventually help identify people who might benefit from preventive treatments. The findings, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association , were based on genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the landmark ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Scientists examined whether differences in participants' genes could help explain why aspirin might affect dementia risk differently from one person to another. The most striking results involved genes associated with platelet count. Platelets are small components of the blood that help form clots, and researchers wanted to determine whether genetic variations related to platelet levels could influence aspirin's potential effects on dementia. After assigning participants genetic scores associated with platelet count, the team compared dementia rates among those who received aspirin and those given a placebo. Among people in the highest 20 percent of platelet count genetic scores, just 1 percent of aspirin users developed dementia, compared with 3.3 percent of participants taking a placebo. That difference translates to approximately a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia among those receiving aspirin. However, the apparent benefit was accompanied by a significant safety concern. In the same genetic group, 4.4 percent of aspirin users experienced major bleeding, compared with 2.1 percent of those receiving a placebo. Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a Research Fellow at Monash's School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the results suggest that a person's genetic makeup could eventually play an important role in determining which dementia prevention strategies are most appropriate. "Previous trials found aspirin didn't prevent dementia when everyone was considered together," Dr. Fransquet said. "In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin. "It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach." The possibility of more targeted prevention is especially important as dementia becomes increasingly common. Dementia Australia estimates that approximately 446,500 people in Australia are living with the condition in 2026. That number is expected to exceed one million by 2065. Previous research has connected dementia with platelet activation and aggregation, the processes through which platelets become active and stick together. However, scientists have had a less complete understanding of how a person's overall platelet count might relate to dementia. The new findings point toward platelet biology as a potentially important area of investigation. Notably, the genetic association identified by researchers did not involve the well-established genetic risk factors typically linked to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. "What's particularly interesting is that the signal wasn't linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and dementia," Dr. Fransquet said. "Instead, it's pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate." Although the findings suggest that aspirin could have different effects depending on a person's genes, researchers emphasize that the results must be confirmed before they can guide medical recommendations. The next step is to investigate whether the association appears in other populations. Scientists would then need to conduct a clinical trial specifically involving people with the genetic profile identified in the analysis. "We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile. "People shouldn't start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding. "If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility." Materials provided by Monash University . https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments. Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land. "These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues." To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans. The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution. "Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum. "It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale." For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments. Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved. "In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said. To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils. One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy. Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate. Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water. The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation. "Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water." Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land. The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America. Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water. Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments. "They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind." The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious. The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits. An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s. "Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming." By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing. The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly. Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived. Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A new study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart, brain, and aging cells through a surprising biological mechanism involving tiny proteins produced by mitochondria, the structures responsible for generating most of the energy our cells need. Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology discovered that people who more closely followed the Mediterranean diet had higher levels of two mitochondrial microproteins called humanin and SHMOOSE. Both have previously been linked to protection against cardiovascular disease and neurodegeneration, the gradual deterioration of nerve cells that occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease. The study, led by USC Leonard Davis Instructional Associate Professor of Gerontology Roberto Vicinanza, offers a possible explanation for how everyday food choices influence cellular health and the aging process. "These microproteins may act as molecular messengers that translate what we eat into how our cells function and age," Vicinanza said. "It's a new biological pathway that helps explain why the Mediterranean diet is so powerful." The Mediterranean diet emphasizes foods such as olive oil, fish, beans, lentils, fruits, and vegetables. It has consistently been associated with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly how this eating pattern produces its wide-ranging health benefits. To investigate, the researchers examined blood samples from older adults who followed the Mediterranean diet to different degrees. Those whose eating habits most closely matched the diet had significantly higher concentrations of humanin and SHMOOSE. They also showed lower indicators of oxidative stress, a process in which harmful molecules called reactive oxygen species overwhelm the body's protective defenses. Over time, oxidative stress can damage proteins, DNA, and other cellular components, contributing to aging and chronic disease. Interestingly, the researchers found that certain foods were associated with different microproteins. Higher consumption of olive oil, fish, and legumes was linked to increased humanin levels. Meanwhile, olive oil consumption and eating fewer refined carbohydrates were associated with higher levels of SHMOOSE. Refined carbohydrates include foods made with heavily processed grains and sugars, such as white bread, pastries, and many sugary snacks. These foods generally contain less fiber and fewer naturally occurring nutrients than their minimally processed counterparts. "These findings suggest that specific components of the Mediterranean diet may directly influence mitochondrial biology," said USC Leonard Davis School Dean and USC Distinguished Professor Pinchas Cohen, the study's senior author. "Humanin and SHMOOSE could serve as biomarkers for adherence to the Mediterranean diet and have clinical significance." Biomarkers are measurable biological indicators that can provide information about a person's health or physiological state. In this case, the researchers suggest that humanin and SHMOOSE could eventually help scientists understand how closely someone's diet aligns with healthy eating patterns and how their cells respond. The findings extend a scientific effort spanning more than 20 years to investigate small proteins produced by mitochondria. Cohen has played a leading role in discovering and studying these molecules, which are increasingly recognized as important participants in cellular health. Mitochondria are often described as the powerhouses of cells because they produce much of the energy required for essential biological activities. But their role extends beyond energy production. They also help regulate metabolism, cellular stress responses, and processes associated with aging. Unlike most proteins, which are produced using instructions stored in the DNA inside the cell's nucleus, mitochondrial microproteins originate from genetic instructions within mitochondria themselves. These instructions are found in small segments of mitochondrial DNA known as open reading frames. Some of these regions were once considered nonfunctional, but researchers have discovered that they can encode biologically active molecules. One of the best understood is humanin, first identified by Cohen and fellow researchers in 2003. Subsequent studies have associated humanin with improved insulin sensitivity, better cardiovascular health, increased longevity, and protection of cognitive abilities. Insulin sensitivity refers to how effectively the body's cells respond to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar. Maintaining healthy insulin sensitivity is important for metabolic health and reducing the risk of type 2 diabetes. Another intriguing microprotein is SHMOOSE (Small Human Mitochondrial ORF Over SErine tRNA), which was identified more recently by Cohen's research team. SHMOOSE has attracted particular interest because of its possible role in protecting the brain. Scientists have found that a genetic variant of SHMOOSE is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. The normal version, meanwhile, appears to help protect neurons from damage involving amyloid, a protein that can accumulate abnormally in the brains of people with Alzheimer's. "These peptides are emerging as key regulators of aging biology," Cohen said. "They connect mitochondrial function to diseases like Alzheimer's and heart disease and now, potentially, to nutrition." The scientists also identified a potentially important connection between humanin and an enzyme called Nox2, which helps generate reactive oxygen species. Although these molecules have useful roles in normal cell signaling and immune defense, excessive production can contribute to oxidative stress and damage blood vessels and other tissues. The researchers observed that people with higher humanin levels tended to have lower Nox2 activity. This relationship raises the possibility that humanin helps limit damaging oxidative processes, potentially offering an additional layer of cardiovascular protection. Based on these findings, the researchers propose that the Mediterranean diet could support heart health in two complementary ways. The diet may help reduce oxidative stress directly while also supporting the production of mitochondrial microproteins that influence pathways involved in cellular damage. However, the observed associations do not establish that the diet directly increases these proteins or that the proteins themselves prevent cardiovascular disease. "This could represent a new cardioprotective mechanism of the Mediterranean diet," Vicinanza said. Vicinanza's interest in the Mediterranean diet extends beyond investigating its effects inside the body. He has also worked to promote this traditional eating pattern internationally as a way to support human health, cultural heritage, and environmental sustainability. As part of those efforts, he collaborated with the Municipality of Pollica in Italy, which is recognized as a UNESCO Mediterranean Diet emblematic community. That collaboration helped support the establishment of the International Day of the Mediterranean Diet through the United Nations. Observed every year on November 16, the international event is intended to draw attention to the Mediterranean diet's health benefits as well as its cultural traditions and environmental significance. For Vicinanza, the new findings reinforce the relationship between traditional food practices and modern discoveries about how the body functions. "We're connecting centuries-old dietary traditions with cutting-edge molecular biology," Vicinanza said. "It supports the idea that healthy eating patterns with little to no ultra-processed foods reflect how humans have eaten over long periods and may create conditions to which mitochondria -- ancient cellular organelles -- are likely adapted."
