https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Being a good listener can sometimes involve more than just listening. It can also mean knowing when and how to say just the right thing—a conversational skill that's invaluable to a crisis counselor.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Nearly 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE, analysis estimates
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: A new study led by Boston University researchers estimates that nearly 75% of all NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) neuropathology. CTE is a neurodegenerative disease that has been diagnosed in individuals with substantial exposure to repetitive head impacts. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Can't sleep? Try this 5-pose yin yoga routine
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: A good night's sleep can feel elusive for many of us, courtesy of a racing mind, a mile-long to-do list and stress getting in the way. What's a tired person to do?

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Arsenic drug combo resurrects 'guardian of the genome' to fight aggressive blood cancers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: A combination cancer therapy that relies on the reactivation of a tumor suppressor protein to kill leukemic and other blood cancer cells has shown promise in a small pilot trial.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: How the tumor environment influences bowel cancer cells' behavior and chemotherapy response
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: New research led by experts at the University of Nottingham has revealed how collagen in the tumor environment can alter bowel cancer cell behavior and influence inflammatory responses to chemotherapy, highlighting potential new avenues for future research into cancer treatment. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research, highlight the importance of the environment surrounding cancer cells in shaping how they behave and respond to treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cell-level analysis reveals how ovarian tumors may develop resistance to chemotherapy
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is an aggressive form of ovarian cancer, characterized in particular by high diversity among the cells that compose a given tumor. This intratumor heterogeneity is a major challenge in understanding why some tumors respond to treatments and others resist. Additionally, this diversity is not limited to genetic differences: tumor cells that have similar genetic profiles may have different functions, depending on the genes they express and their epigenetic state.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-j.title: Japan's telemedicine use increased from 2020 to 2024 as age gap widened
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-j.summary: Telemedicine came into wide use during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, access to and use of telemedicine may vary according to factors such as age, educational attainment, income, employment status and place of residence, though it has long been unclear whether these disparities would narrow as the use of telemedicine spread.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Researchers develop privacy-friendly, secure and sustainable AI techniques for medical imaging
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Artificial intelligence can be helpful in analyzing medical images and support radiotherapy planning workflows. However, huge amounts of sensitive patient data are needed to train robust AI models. Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have investigated how hospitals can jointly develop AI models for radiation therapy applications without exchanging such data. In their project, they use federated learning, a process in which a single model is trained at a decentralized location while the data remains in place. Their results demonstrate not only the technical feasibility of the approach but also its safe, more sustainable, and accessible use.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: How a neurologist is rethinking stroke prevention for the longevity era
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: For decades, stroke prevention has revolved around a list of separate—and often separately treated—risk factors: blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and inactivity. According to Dr. Gustavo Saposnik, it's time to start considering biological age as a risk factor for stroke.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Running distance is associated with how female runners distribute their daily energy expenditure
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Generally, total energy expenditure is expected to be higher in individuals with greater physical activity. However, the constrained total energy expenditure model suggests that greater energy expenditure during exercise may be offset by lower energy expenditure during other activities or physiological processes, thereby maintaining total energy expenditure within a relatively limited range. It is unclear whether similar patterns occur in athletes engaged in long-term endurance training.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Animal and plant proteins show different associations with testosterone levels in men
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Higher animal protein intake was associated with lower blood testosterone levels, while higher plant protein intake was associated with higher levels, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland. The findings were published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Preclinical research shows macrophages can be programmed to fight solid cancer tumors
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: One person dies every 50 seconds in the U.S. from cancer, and an estimated 39% of people in the country will develop cancer during their lifetime. Survival rates have improved in recent decades from innovations and combinations of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and biotechnology. Still, some cancers resist treatment or recur.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Don't let Halloween scare your heart health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Halloween season is a time for scary tricks and sweet treats. But people with heart conditions may need to take extra precautions before participating in fright nights. Baylor College of Medicine cardiologist and electrophysiologist Dr. Mohamed Gabr explains what you need to know to keep your heart healthy during this spooky season.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Fighting cancer also means fighting against social stigma
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Cancer-related discrimination arises from long-lasting cultural and institutional misconceptions, with significant impacts on every part of a person's quality of life and health—and Flinders University researchers say it requires coordinated policy, legal, institutional and public education responses for change to occur.

https://theconversation.com/1-in-4-penns.title: 1 in 4 Pennsylvanians say they paid out of pocket for their annual checkup. Why isn’t insurance covering these preventive visits?
https://theconversation.com/1-in-4-penns.summary: Billing errors, testing and questions about new symptoms can lead to unexpected bills, making some patients wary to go back for their next checkup.

https://theconversation.com/some-states-.title: Some states are stepping up after federal childcare cuts – and now offer lessons for the future
https://theconversation.com/some-states-.summary: Improving both supply and quality of childcare has been the focus of several states trying to find solutions on their own.

https://theconversation.com/falcon-9-ush.title: Falcon 9 ushered in the modern space economy – retiring it could leave the industry vulnerable
https://theconversation.com/falcon-9-ush.summary: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket has allowed NASA, private companies, universities and nonprofits alike to launch satellites, spacecraft and even astronauts to orbit.

https://theconversation.com/let-nothing-.title: ‘Let nothing be forgotten’: Holocaust survivors’ memorial books honored lives lost and vibrant hometowns
https://theconversation.com/let-nothing-.summary: After the Holocaust, Eastern European survivors collaborated on memorial books called ‘yizker bikher’ – one way to reclaim their neighbors’ lives and memories.

https://theconversation.com/plans-with-c.title: Plans with cheaper premiums are risky business for Americans seeking lower healthcare costs
https://theconversation.com/plans-with-c.summary: Some options that might look like health insurance actually aren’t – and they may leave you stranded with large, unexpected medical expenses.

https://theconversation.com/why-over-two.title: Why over two-thirds of Americans say their country is in decline
https://theconversation.com/why-over-two.summary: A recent national survey reveals a US electorate that is unsettled, gloomy and likely looking for political change.

https://theconversation.com/ive-been-tal.title: I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not
https://theconversation.com/ive-been-tal.summary: Despite the headwinds that have cratered support for Donald Trump – high prices, the Iran war, corruption – many of Trump’s MAGA loyalists still back him. A scholar who studies MAGA looks at why.

https://theconversation.com/pittsburghs-.title: Pittsburgh’s ‘Green Man’ was a real person – why the legend outlives the facts
https://theconversation.com/pittsburghs-.summary: He wasn’t a monster. He was just a man who survived a terrible accident. So why won’t western Pennsylvania let go of its ‘Green Man’ legend? A folklorist explains.

https://theconversation.com/ai-may-quick.title: AI may quickly generate ideas, but working with people leads to more creative ones
https://theconversation.com/ai-may-quick.summary: A recent experiment found that people working with ChatGPT generated fewer unique ideas than those who collaborated with other humans.

https://theconversation.com/new-restrict.title: New restrictions on purchases with SNAP benefits in some states mean fewer convenience stores are accepting them
https://theconversation.com/new-restrict.summary: Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a big burden for retailers.

https://theconversation.com/private-equi.title: Private equity is buying up more methadone clinics – access to the lifesaving drug isn’t getting easier
https://theconversation.com/private-equi.summary: Despite acquiring more than one-third of US methadone clinics, private equity has not significantly expanded methadone availability.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic.title: Optimistic climate futures for local communities in the UK imagined in a new report
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic.summary: A new report co-authored by researchers from the University of York and WWF highlights how local communities across the U.K. imagine positive, sustainable, and resilient futures for the places where they live and work.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-oce.title: How the Indian Ocean is linked to Europe's early-winter rain and storms
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-oce.summary: When we think about Europe's winter weather, the Indian Ocean is probably not the first place we look. We might picture Atlantic storms, cold air arriving from the north or rain sweeping across the Mediterranean. In my research, however, I look at how these familiar weather systems fit into a much larger climate system. My colleagues and I asked whether an ocean thousands of kilometers away could leave a detectable signature on Europe's early winter.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-li.title: The phantom lighthouse: New research explains one of Australia's strangest illusions
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-li.summary: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The first was built in 1873, but was decommissioned in 1995 when the second took over the job of warning ships off the reef. Visitors to the island, however, regularly report seeing signs of a third lighthouse. At night the beams of a nonexistent phantom lighthouse are seen far off, shining on the horizon.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.summary: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-mag.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-mag.summary: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolec.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolec.summary: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-.summary: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-difference.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-difference.summary: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-decodin.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-decodin.summary: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chornobyl-.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chornobyl-.summary: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gen-artifi.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gen-artifi.summary: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-radical-pa.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-radical-pa.summary: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-schools-af.title: Schools increasingly affected by poor air quality as wildfire smoke becomes more common
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-schools-af.summary: American children are increasingly exposed to air pollution as wildfire smoke becomes more common, and some schools and child care centers struggle to keep indoor breathing conditions clean, a new national study shows.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-medieval-g.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon‑stealing spirits
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-medieval-g.summary: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rarely-dee.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rarely-dee.summary: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-drones-wea.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-drones-wea.summary: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gibberelli.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gibberelli.summary: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-year-myste.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-year-myste.summary: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tissue-atl.title: New tissue atlas aims to help AI understand cancer
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tissue-atl.summary: How cells are arranged within tissue can reveal as much about disease as the cells themselves. When doctors examine a cancer tumor, for example, they don't just look at which cells are present; they also want to know how those cells are arranged and how they interact with each other. That's because the way cancer cells interact with neighboring immune cells can offer important clues about how a disease develops or responds to treatment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-relocating.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-relocating.summary: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sun-outer-.title: Sun's outer magnetic field mapped in 3D for the first time
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sun-outer-.summary: A team of researchers has produced the first global, three-dimensional estimates of the sun's magnetic field, including the area beyond the sun's visible edge. This marks a step toward more accurate models of solar activity—and ultimately, better predictions of solar magnetic eruptions, which are the root cause of extreme space weather that can impact critical infrastructure technologies on Earth.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-physics-ai.title: A new physics-informed AI tool aims to predict wildfire spread in real time and assist wildfire response
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-physics-ai.summary: A new AI system that NYU Fire Research Group describes as a digital twin of an active wildfire has, in early testing, shown the ability to forecast how a fire will spread in near real time.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-customizab.title: Customizable DNA labels can selectively guide drug carriers to cancer cells
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-customizab.summary: Cells naturally send tiny packages to one another to share information. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have developed a simple, low-cost way to turn those packages into drug carriers that can deliver treatments directly to cancer cells, potentially improving effectiveness while reducing side effects.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-humidity-p.title: Humidity can change how smoke pollutants transform after dark
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-humidity-p.summary: What happens to smoke particles after sunset can depend strongly on something as familiar as the amount of water in the air. New research from Md. Sohel Rana and Marcelo I. Guzman at the University of Kentucky shows that relative humidity can redirect the chemical pathways involved in the nighttime oxidation of catechol, a phenolic compound associated with biomass burning.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-forgotten-.title: 'Let nothing be forgotten': Holocaust survivors' memorial books honored lives lost and vibrant hometowns
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-forgotten-.summary: My grandmother was a Holocaust survivor from Kostopol, Ukraine. Years after she passed away, I was trying to learn more about her life before the war—something I knew very little about. When I found a book called "Sefer Kostopol"—Hebrew for "Book of Kostopol"—I hoped to find her among its pages.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists count more than 2 million eels on one underwater mountain
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Patience Seamount is an underwater mountain in Australia's Huon Marine Park off the coast of Tasmania. Every year, it is the site of an enormous gathering of basketwork eels (Diastobranchus capensis) for reasons unknown, although most likely to spawn. The numbers are huge, but they have never been quantified.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-celebrity-.title: Study finds celebrity digital twins may boost trust in customer service
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-celebrity-.summary: Imagine losing your credit card, logging into your bank's website for help and being greeted by a virtual customer service representative who looks and sounds exactly like actor Hugh Jackman. The person helping you isn't actually the Hollywood star—it's his AI-powered digital twin. And new research suggests that familiar face could significantly improve how you perceive your customer service experience.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gambling-t.title: Gambling risks found among teens as young as 13
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gambling-t.summary: More than half (52.5%) of Americans ages 13 to 27 reported gambling in the past year, including 42.7% of teens ages 13 to 17, according to researchers at the Center for Gambling Studies at the Rutgers School of Social Work.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-childhood-.title: How childhood experiences shape employment outcomes in India
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-childhood-.summary: Research led by the University of East Anglia (UEA) shows that childhood poverty, poor living conditions and gender can have lasting impacts on employment opportunities and earnings in India.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-uv-scans-u.title: UV scans uncover natural varnish that may have preserved ancient Chauvet Cave drawings
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-uv-scans-u.summary: Tucked away inside a limestone cave in southeastern France lies some of the oldest artwork in existence. Known as Chauvet Cave, the site is so historically important—and fragile—that its location is kept secret and the cave is locked behind a huge steel door. And now, researchers have devised a technique to safely investigate these artworks and understand the natural varnish that has protected them for centuries. Their findings are published in the journal ACS Omega.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Can an AI chatbot help women recognize heart disease?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: HeartBot, created by a team of UC researchers, regularly answers questions from women seeking information on heart disease. The project was led by Yoshimi Fukuoka, Ph.D., RN, FAAN, a nurse scientist and professor at UC San Francisco's School of Nursing. The goal was to study whether having a heart-health chatbot on their phone would increase study participants' awareness of heart disease risks and recognition of heart attack symptoms so they would seek medical help when necessary.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: Recommendations developed for management of hidradenitis suppurativa
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: Evidence-based recommendations are presented for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) in guidelines of care issued by the American Academy of Dermatology and the Hidradenitis Suppurativa Foundation and published online Oct. 20 in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-v.title: Video decision aid increases advance care planning in seniors with chronic kidney disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-v.summary: Among older adults with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), a video decision aid increases advance care planning (ACP) documentation in the electronic health record, according to a study published in JAMA Internal Medicine to coincide with Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Achilles injections show no meaningful benefit over sham treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Commonly used injections for Achilles tendinopathy—pain, stiffness and swelling in the Achilles tendon—offer no meaningful clinical advantage over placebo (sham) treatment, finds a clinical trial published by The BMJ.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Corridor care is hiding the true scale of the NHS hospital crisis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: The label "corridor care" is hiding the true scale of the NHS hospital crisis, warns a senior doctor in The BMJ today.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Measles outbreak that contributed to Canada losing elimination status highlights risks from persistent immunity gaps
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: The outbreak that contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025 was concentrated in historically undervaccinated communities with close social networks across Canada, the U.S., Mexico and beyond, creating opportunities for cross-border transmission, concludes a study published by The BMJ.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Wider surgical margins may not mean better cancer control
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: It's a question that surgeons often face: How much surrounding healthy tissue should they take out when removing a patient's cancer to be sure it is fully eliminated? Removing more can sacrifice nearby nerves, blood vessels, tendons and even joints, with lasting effects on quality of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mutated immune cells raise red flags in lupus
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) have discovered that patients with lupus have unusual mutations that may turn their bodies into battlegrounds.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Smarter CAR-T cells could beat a deadly pediatric brain cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Scientists at UC San Francisco have engineered CAR-T cells that stay dormant until they reach the brain, where they switch on and destroy tumor cells. In mice, these CAR-T cells were able to clear diffuse midline glioma (DMG), a lethal form of childhood brain cancer that integrates into healthy tissue. The cells also had staying power. When scientists introduced another round of cancer several weeks later, the cells were still able to fight.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: CDC names the 4 most dangerous superbugs in the US
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Superbugs cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Large-scale genetic study on Alzheimer's identifies new DNA risks
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: A large-scale international study offers new insights for understanding Alzheimer's disease and developing future treatments. The University of Exeter–led PROTECT study was part of the research, led by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and published in Nature, which sheds clearer light on the role of immune cells within the brain, as well as several specific neuronal cell types.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Biological mechanism underlying Huntington's disease may be more widespread in the brain than previously thought
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: In 2025, a team of scientists revealed some unexpected findings about how the inherited DNA repeat associated with Huntington's disease causes the illness—by slowly expanding throughout a person's life, then becoming toxic after enlarging to several times its original length. The findings were in a specific brain region, the striatum, but it wasn't clear if the same process was directly causing the harm in other parts of the brain affected by the disease.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: How sex-based biology shapes the brain's response to injury
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Injury-induced stress cascades through the body by activating immune responses, shifting energy away from less urgent concerns to prioritize healing. In traumatic brain injury, or TBI, the brain—home to the signaling hubs that manage those safety processes—is the site of the incident.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Deep brain stimulation in patients with epilepsy produces measurable response within minutes, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have detected measurable changes in the brain within 18 minutes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in people with drug-resistant epilepsy, a finding that could eventually help clinicians personalize treatment without waiting months to determine whether stimulation settings are effective. The study was recently published in iScience.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health. A study published in Neurology , the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes. Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages. "Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil. Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss. To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years. At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners. Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda. Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes. Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information. Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time. High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least. After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group. That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period. Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging. These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems. Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants. Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60. The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake. Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory. Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol. Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners. The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain. "While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives." Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes. In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption. The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences. Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes. The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition. The findings, published in General Psychiatry , point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health. To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia. The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk. Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors. Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study. "Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China. Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation. Materials provided by Wiley . https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay. Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health. Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health. Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells. Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities. Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume. "Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said. To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water. "It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry. On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth. After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing. Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period. The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples. Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities. The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids. Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context. "Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said. Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health. Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay. Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness. "But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable." The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports . https://phys.org/news/2026-10-people-eye.title: Why people turn a blind eye to prisoner abuse
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-people-eye.summary: Common beliefs that people who commit crime are inherently bad and unlikely to change may make the public more accepting of illegitimate harms within the criminal justice system, according to criminology and psychology experts in the U.S. and Australia.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-evolved-al.title: Heat-evolved algae offer clues to helping corals withstand warming seas
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-evolved-al.summary: A research team led by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) has found that heat-evolved algae maintain more stable biomolecular profiles under elevated temperatures than their non-evolved (wild-type) counterparts, providing new insights into how they withstand heat stress.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-cosmic-mic.title: Cosmic microwave background offers evidence of gas flowing in galaxy clusters
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-cosmic-mic.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is a faint glow in the universe dating back to roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang, long before stars or galaxies emerged. Detecting this light and mapping its fluctuations provide valuable insights into the age and composition of the universe.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-capturing-.title: Capturing our closest archaeal relatives offers clues to the origin of eukaryotes
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-capturing-.summary: A collaborative research team led by Hiroyuki Imachi and Masaru K. Nobu of the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) and Satoshi Nakagawa of Kyoto University has for the first time isolated and cultivated two strains of Heimdallarchaeia, a group of archaea that are among the closest known archaeal relatives of eukaryotes—the organisms that include humans and other animals, as well as plants and fungi.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rainfall-m.title: Rainfall can travel from mountain slopes to rivers far faster than expected in mountain catchments
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rainfall-m.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba have found that river responses to rainfall can reach rivers and appear as runoff much more rapidly than previously assumed in mountainous regions. Through continuous monitoring of precipitation and river water levels, they documented rapid rainfall-related responses not only in moderate-relief catchments but also in high-relief catchments with mountain slopes exceeding 500 m in length. The findings provide new insights into runoff generation and flood development in mountainous regions. The paper is published in the Journal of Hydrology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-ch.title: Ancient charcoal remains provide clues about Neanderthal camp organization
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-ch.summary: Usually, people associate archaeological studies with bones, pottery and primitive tools, but archaeologists often find other clues about how ancient people lived hidden throughout a site. A new study, published in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology, focuses on bits of charcoal and their spatial organization to get a glimpse of Neanderthal life in Abric Romaní, an ancient rock shelter near Barcelona.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-universiti.title: How universities can help deliver global biodiversity goals
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-universiti.summary: "Taking Action for Nature" was the theme of CoP 17, the UN Biodiversity Conference 2026, which is drawing to a close in Yerevan, Armenia. A new analysis of African national biodiversity strategies and action plans shows how academic and research institutions can respond to this theme and help translate scientific evidence into taking action for nature.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-enormous-c.title: Enormous 'Cat's Tail' tells of cosmic collision 63 light-years away
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-enormous-c.summary: Sixty-three light-years from Earth, in the small, faint constellation known as Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"), there lies a strange structure that has puzzled astronomers for the last two years. Nicknamed the "Cat's Tail," this dark feature stretches across an abyss of space about a thousand times the average distance between Earth and the sun.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tropical-p.title: New tropical protea flowers expand floriculture opportunities across Hawaiʻi
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tropical-p.summary: Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience (CTAHR) have bred new "tropical" pincushion protea (Leucospermum) hybrids that bloom near sea level, reducing local reliance on imported flowers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-grand-thef.title: Grand Theft Astro: Stars' criminal histories could reshape estimates of their internal magnetic fields
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-grand-thef.summary: Magnetic fields exist in many stars, including the sun. Yet they remain too poorly understood to be reliably included in stellar evolution models, limiting their accuracy. Now, a new study by researchers at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, shows why a star's "criminal" evolutionary history may be crucial for correctly interpreting its internal magnetic fields.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.title: Ultrathin carbon ribbons conduct electricity like metals in first successful synthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.summary: As modern electronic devices shrink, so do the metal electrical wires inside them. However, they start to run into serious problems the smaller they get. Conventional wires generate excessive heat and suffer a massive spike in electrical resistance that affects overall performance.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-underprepa.title: Underpreparing for severe climate risks can cost the UK far more than overpreparing, experts warn
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-underprepa.summary: Experts in climate, nature, health, national security, and financial risk have joined forces to call for a more integrated approach to government climate and nature risk assessments. In a commentary published in Nature Climate Change, they warn that conflicting advice can give policymakers very different pictures of the severity of the risks ahead, making it harder to judge how seriously to act and how much to spend.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-brighter-e.title: Brighter evenings, darker school mornings: Permanent daylight saving time could put children's safety at risk
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-brighter-e.summary: In July 2026, the U.S. House passed legislation to make daylight saving time (DST) permanent. But a new analysis of the consequences of the Sunshine Protection Act, reported in the journal Current Biology on Oct. 29, finds that this legislation would have serious safety consequences for millions of schoolchildren across the U.S. They would have to leave for school before sunrise, when fatal crashes involving pedestrians are more likely, for much of the school year.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-forest.htm.title: What makes forest protection work?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-forest.htm.summary: A new study from the Institute for Food and Resource Economics at the University of Bonn shows that the success of nature conservation measures depends partly on the credible enforcement of environmental laws.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-theoretica.title: Theoretical method uses light to locate anyons, potential quantum computing building blocks
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-theoretica.summary: Theoretical physicists at Emory University have discovered a way to use light to detect the "spectral fingerprints" of anyons—exotic quasiparticles that emerge from the collective behavior of many electrons. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters. The work offers a new tool for the study of anyons, which hold potential as fundamental building blocks for quantum computing.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-fossil-sca.title: New fossil scans challenge insect flight timeline, suggesting origins up to 80 million years later
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-fossil-sca.summary: A tiny fossil discovered exactly a century ago has caused an enormous change in our understanding of when flying insects first appeared on Earth.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mathematic.title: New mathematical method improves calculations for systems limited by their smallest input
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mathematic.summary: A harmonic increment provides a new way to improve smooth approximations of the minimum function. In a recent paper, published in the Journal of Inequalities and Applications, Prof. Thomas A. Weber shows how a harmonic-increment transformation brings any smooth estimate that lies strictly below the minimum closer to it, while keeping the improved estimate below the minimum, so it remains a conservative estimate of a worst realization, or weakest link.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-museum-spe.title: Museum specimens reveal shrinking flying foxes in Madagascar, with commercial hunting suspected
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-museum-spe.summary: Flying foxes are the biggest bats in the world; they look like German shepherd puppies with 5-foot (1.5-meter) wingspans. But Madagascar's flying foxes are shrinking.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-al.title: Ancient Alberta fish fossils reveal evolutionary secrets of modern species
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-al.summary: Rare, complete fossils of ancient fish discovered in Alberta are helping fill in the gaps in our knowledge about which freshwater fish were living in North America at the end of the age of the dinosaurs, and how they evolved into their modern descendants.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-modest-gam.title: Modest gamma-ray flash followed by dazzling afterglow points to powerful stellar jet viewed off-axis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-modest-gam.summary: A cosmic explosion that announced itself with a modest flash of gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. An international team of astronomers now finds evidence that the surprising mismatch comes down to perspective: Earth was outside the most intensely beamed light from the explosion.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indoor-air.title: Indoor plants could improve air quality and cooling
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indoor-air.summary: In a study published in Eco-Environment and Health, a team of 35 international experts led by Surrey's Global Centre for Clean Air Research (GCARE) reviewed several studies from across the world on the performance of indoor greenery.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-a.title: Using hydrogen to spark ammonia engines into life
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-a.summary: "Ammonia was first used as a fuel during World War II, when gasoline was hard to get hold of," explains David Emberson, associate professor at NTNU's Department of Marine Technology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-saharan-ba.title: Saharan dust carries desert bacteria across the Atlantic to Amazon rainforest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-saharan-ba.summary: Viewed under a microscope, the air above the Amazon rainforest teems with activity. It is full of pollen, fungal spores, tiny plant particles and bacteria. Normally, the composition of this bioaerosol community is quite stable. A team that included researchers from the University of Graz, the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz and Brazilian partner institutions has now shown that microorganisms are transported across the Atlantic along with desert dust from the Sahara.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-children-a.title: Children need to learn to swim for academic and social milestones, rather than just fitness, research suggests
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-children-a.summary: With family budgets stretched ever tighter, swimming lessons can be one of the first expenses to be cut back—but with research showing swimming helps children not just physically but developmentally, researchers are calling for greater government support.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: 5 calisthenics moves for a full-body workout you can do anywhere
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Whether you realize it or not, you're probably already familiar with calisthenics. Put simply, calisthenics is just bodyweight exercises. Calisthenics is great for beginners because it builds full-body strength and requires no equipment. You can also easily modify exercises for different levels of difficulty.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: STI screening linked to fewer preterm births
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Screening and treating pregnant patients for three common sexually transmitted infections (STIs) twice during pregnancy was associated with a 23% lower risk of preterm birth compared with standard care, according to a randomized clinical trial published in Clinical Infectious Diseases from researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Southern California.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Older brains cope better with lack of sleep, says study
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.summary: A new Simon Fraser University study suggests that brains in healthy older adults may cope better with a lack of sleep than those in younger adults.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-v.title: Vitamin-carrying protein pathway shows promise for brain drug delivery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-v.summary: Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have identified a transporter protein with the potential to open new avenues for improving creatine delivery into the brain and for developing other therapies targeting the central nervous system.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Magnetic bead implants could offer more accurate way to control prosthetic limbs
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: MIT researchers have shown that they can accurately track muscle movement using tiny magnetic beads implanted in the muscle. These measurements could make it easier for people with certain types of amputations to control their prosthetic limbs.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Genetic testing may help identify inherited blood disorder carrier status earlier
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have found that genetic testing can help identify people who carry inherited blood disorder traits, including individuals who may not otherwise know their carrier status. Earlier identification can create opportunities for genetic counseling, informed family planning and appropriate clinical follow-up.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Iron-based MRI agent detects and slows heart scarring in lab-grown human tissue
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: The Biomolecular Nanotechnology research group led by Ikerbasque research professor Aitziber L. Cortajarena has developed a new iron-based contrast agent for magnetic resonance imaging that can be used for both diagnosis and treatment. In a study carried out on lab-grown human heart tissue, it was proven that the contrast agent accumulates in the fibrotic tissue, that its signal intensity on the MRI image increases with the severity of the disease, and that it slows disease progression.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: What brain scans can reveal, and why they don't always explain symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: In 2007, researchers in the Netherlands scanned the brains of 2,000 people aged 45 and over who were going about their ordinary lives. Seven in every 100 had signs of a stroke they never knew they'd had. Nearly two in 100 had a small bulge in a blood vessel, and a similar number had a tumor that appeared to be benign, meaning it was not cancerous.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: A hidden brain rhythm challenges ideas about where consciousness comes from
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: How our brains give rise to consciousness is one of the biggest mysteries in neuroscience. But new research by Janis Hesse at the University of California, Berkeley, and colleagues, may help fill in some of the details. The insights are coming from studies on macaque monkeys.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Permanent daylight saving time could add at least two billion dark school commutes across US
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill this past summer that would make daylight saving time (DST) permanent in the United States—meaning there would be no turning back the clocks each fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already preapproved this change. If the bill is ultimately signed into law, the change would go into effect in those states.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: GLP-1 drugs may help patients shed regained weight after bariatric surgery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: People who regain weight after bariatric surgery may benefit from glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly called GLP-1 medications, according to a study involving Regenstrief Institute, Indiana University, Purdue University and University of Florida researchers. The study found that patients prescribed these medications lost more of their regained weight over six and 12 months than comparable patients who did not use them.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: New research warns of the possible cybercrime pitfalls for autistic people
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Autistic adults may have elevated risks of being involved in cyber-related crime, with Flinders University experts warning that these people might fall into such crimes unwittingly.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: Excessive polypharmacy and complex medication regimens are associated with greater physician burden
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: Patients receiving home-based medical care are often older adults with multiple chronic conditions, and polypharmacy, commonly defined as the concurrent use of multiple medications, is prevalent in this population. However, the challenges of medication management extend beyond the number of prescribed medications.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Nearly half of severely distressed generative AI users turn to chatbots for emotional support, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: A new study has found that almost one in three Israeli adults surveyed who use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools reported seeking emotional support, coping advice or mental health assistance from platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini. Among users experiencing severe psychological distress, that figure rose to nearly one in two, according to researchers from Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and collaborating institutions.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Researchers identify critical window for boosting immunotherapy response in prostate cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Researchers at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center have shown that hormone-blocking therapies commonly used to treat prostate cancers temporarily activate the body's immune response before those immune effects begin to fade over time. In a new publication in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer, a team led by Kent Nastiuk, Ph.D., reports this discovery—and points the way to a treatment strategy for taking advantage of this window of opportunity.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: Halting muscular dystrophy with a 'backup' protein
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: A new use of CRISPR gene editing has halted and even reversed the progression of a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, according to work led by scientists at the Perelman School of Medicine. The technique boosted a protein, utrophin, as a stand-in to take on the job of a different protein, dystrophin, which helps maintain healthy muscles and is in short supply in those with muscular dystrophy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Why daylight saving time may be bad for your brain and health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Turning the clocks back an hour each fall can feel like a gift: an extra hour of sleep. But the trade-off is less daylight in the evening, and the annual switch continues to earn mixed reviews. The same is true in spring, when we lose an hour as daylight saving time begins.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Colorectal cancer in younger patients shows distinct cellular and gene-activity patterns
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, along with researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published in Nature Medicine, the study—the largest of its kind—lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Immune changes linked to diabetes could guide development of new cancer treatments
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: New research in The Journal of Immunology uncovers how high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) and type 1 diabetes (T1D) may protect against certain cancers like melanoma, breast and colon cancer. T1D has been associated with a decreased risk of certain cancers, but the exact reasons why have remained a mystery. New data from studies in mice now show that it could be due to changes in immune cells, called T cells, caused by hyperglycemia.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.title: Universal immunization of newborns against RSV could significantly reduce infant hospitalizations in EU
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.summary: As the season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory diseases approaches, a new report from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) indicates that universal immunization of newborns against RSV could substantially reduce hospitalizations among infants linked to the disease during the winter season.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Meal delivery apps could be driving us toward unhealthy choices
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: New research has revealed how meal delivery apps are steering Australians toward unhealthy food options, prompting calls from experts for government action to reset the balance and make choosing healthy options easier and more affordable.

https://theconversation.com/what-is-shar.title: What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
https://theconversation.com/what-is-shar.summary: Ordinary Muslim religious practices can often be treated as political threats, writes a law professor.

https://theconversation.com/political-in.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
https://theconversation.com/political-in.summary: Younger Americans’ pop culture favorites have multipartisan appeal, but male creators dominate the list of top influencers, podcasters and comedians.

https://theconversation.com/democrats-ar.title: Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies
https://theconversation.com/democrats-ar.summary: A quiet US-Mexico border, and the reduced urgency of undocumented immigration, has deprived Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

https://theconversation.com/we-discovere.title: We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?
https://theconversation.com/we-discovere.summary: This amoeba lives at hotter temperatures than any other eukaryote previously discovered.

https://theconversation.com/driverless-1.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
https://theconversation.com/driverless-1.summary: Chaotic roads are still too difficult for automated trucks to navigate.

https://theconversation.com/faculty-and-.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
https://theconversation.com/faculty-and-.summary: Some universities are developing innovative arrangements with media outlets where students help report and faculty provide guidance.

https://theconversation.com/who-mapped-a.title: Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent
https://theconversation.com/who-mapped-a.summary: African guides drew lines in the sand to help Europeans understand the terrain. But they rarely got the credit.

https://theconversation.com/how-the-law-.title: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
https://theconversation.com/how-the-law-.summary: A handful of providers are hijacking the arbitration process – and consumers are likely to foot the bill.

https://theconversation.com/federal-poli.title: Federal policy helped widen rural America’s fresh food gap, but a 90-year-old law could help close it
https://theconversation.com/federal-poli.summary: A food systems researcher shows how trucking deregulation and lax antitrust enforcement let big grocery chains grow as rural distribution thinned.

https://theconversation.com/king-charles.title: King Charles’ visit to the Caribbean evokes specter of British slavery – and local demands for justice
https://theconversation.com/king-charles.summary: For locals, the king’s Caribbean visit is an occasion to recognize the full story of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of millions of people across the Atlantic.
